question:
A 48-year-old male presents with progressive dyspnea over 4 months, initially occurring with stair
climbing but now present at rest. His medical history includes hypertension managed with lisinopril and
gastric cancer treated with chemotherapy and surgery 11 months ago. He denies smoking, alcohol
use, or illicit drug use. Physical examination reveals: - Height: 183 cm, weight: 68 kg (BMI: 20 kg/m2) -
Respiratory rate: 22/min, other vitals normal - O2 saturation: 96% on room air - Jugular venous
distension - Mild hepatomegaly - Bilateral 2+ pitting lower extremity edema - Loud P2 - Grade 2/6
holosystolic murmur at left sternal border - Diffuse bilateral pulmonary bruits that increase with
inspiration Diagnostic findings include: - Normal serum studies and urinalysis - Chest x-ray: enlarged
pulmonary trunk, prominent right heart border, decreased vascular markings - Echocardiogram: right
ventricular dilation and hypertrophy, right atrial dilation, tricuspid regurgitation - Normal spirometry -
Right heart catheterization: mean pulmonary arterial pressure 30 mm Hg (N: 10-20), pulmonary
capillary wedge pressure 10 mm Hg (N: 5-16) What is the most likely cause of these cardiac
catheterization findings? Answer Choices: (A) Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (B)
Pulmonary veno-occlusive disease (C) Portal pulmonary hypertension (D) Primary pulmonary arterial
hypertension (E) Chemotherapy-induced cardiomyopathy (F) Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (G)
Scleroderma-associated pulmonary arterial hypertension (H) Eisenmenger syndrome (I) Recurrent
pulmonary embolism (J) Left ventricular diastolic dysfunction
 A. Primary pulmonary arterial hypertension
B. Pulmonary veno-occlusive disease
C. Eisenmenger syndrome
D. Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension
E. Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction
F. Portal pulmonary hypertension
G. Chemotherapy-induced cardiomyopathy
H. Left ventricular diastolic dysfunction
I. Recurrent pulmonary embolism
J. Scleroderma-associated pulmonary arterial hypertension
